nameStory: Johnson grass gets its name from Colonel William Johnson, an Alabama plantation owner who planted it on his river-bottom farmland around 1840. Ironically, the grass was already growing wild in several states by then, so the Colonel just helped spread what would become one of America's most notorious weeds!
description: Johnson grass is a tall, robust grass that can tower over your head, reaching 3-8 feet high. It forms dense clumps with broad, corn-like leaves and produces large, open flower clusters that look like reddish-brown plumes at the top of sturdy stems. This aggressive plant spreads both by underground stems called rhizomes and by seeds, allowing it to quickly take over disturbed areas and farm fields.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large, open, pyramid-shaped flower clusters (panicles) at stem tips, often reddish-brown to purplish, feeling somewhat rough to the touch and reaching 6-20 inches long

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Broad, flat blades resembling corn leaves, smooth to slightly rough, with a prominent white midrib running down the center and feeling somewhat waxy

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, tall clumps 3-8 feet high, spreading aggressively by underground runners to create large patches

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, reddish-brown seeds that feel hard and smooth, produced abundantly in the large flower clusters

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, sturdy stems that feel solid and smooth, often with a slight waxy coating and reddish tinge at the joints

habitat: In New England, Johnson grass thrives in disturbed, fertile soils along roadsides, field edges, abandoned farmland, and streambanks. It prefers sunny, open areas with rich, moist soil and is most commonly found in agricultural areas or places where soil has been recently disturbed.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from underground rhizomes, growing rapidly into tall clumps of broad, corn-like leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with full height reached and distinctive reddish-brown flower plumes appearing at stem tops, usually from July through August.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and disperse while leaves may turn yellow or brown. Frost-damaged foliage becomes potentially toxic to livestock.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back, but underground rhizomes survive to sprout new growth in spring.

funFact: Johnson grass produces hydrogen cyanide when stressed by drought or frost, making it potentially deadly to cattle and horses - nature's own chemical warfare system that can actually poison the animals that try to eat it!
confusionNotes: Johnson grass is most easily confused with cultivated sorghum or corn in its early stages, but its aggressive clumping growth habit and distinctive open, reddish flower clusters set it apart. Remember: if it's forming dense patches in wild areas rather than neat farm rows, it's likely Johnson grass.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called Johnson grass after its supposed Alabama introducer, this plant was actually brought to America accidentally and was already established before Colonel Johnson ever planted it. It's considered one of the world's ten worst weeds and is illegal to transport in 19 U.S. states.
compareHints: Johnson grass differs from its cultivated cousin grain sorghum by its much more aggressive spreading habit and smaller seeds. While grain sorghum grows as individual plants from planted seeds, Johnson grass forms dense colonies through underground runners and readily escapes cultivation to become weedy.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Sorghum differs from its notorious relative Johnson grass by being an annual that grows from seed each year rather than a perennial that spreads by underground rhizomes.
